title: Tzav: first, the ashes (Leviticus 6:3–4)
hookLine: each day the priest begins by clearing yesterday's ashes, in plain clothes

lines: THE FIRST JOB OF THE DAY.
cards: In the sanctuary, as the rabbis describe the day, the first job wasn't a grand prayer or a beautiful offering. It was cleaning.
Before anything new could happen on the altar, someone had to deal with what was left from yesterday. The fire had burned all night, and there were ashes.
And the Torah gives that humble job careful instructions, right down to what the priest should wear.

teach.h: LINEN AT THE ALTAR, PLAIN CLOTHES OUTSIDE.
teach.b: The priest puts on his linen priestly garments, lifts a portion of the ashes from the altar and sets it beside the altar.
Then he takes off those garments, puts on others, and carries the rest of the ashes out of the camp, to a clean place.
The rabbis called this terumat ha-deshen, the lifting of the ashes, and it was the first act of the Temple day. Notice the two changes of clothes.
Lifting the ashes at the altar is done in full priestly linen: this dirty job counts as holy service. For hauling them out, the priest changes into plainer clothes.

Rashi explains with a picture from a household: the clothes a servant wears to cook a pot for his master aren't the clothes he wears to pour his master's wine. Each job gets the right clothes, and both are service.
Then the Mishnah adds a story.
In the Temple, this job was so sought after that priests would race up the ramp of the altar to win it; whoever got within four cubits first won.
Once, two were neck and neck, one pushed the other, and he fell and broke his leg.
After that, the court decided it by lottery. Grown men, competing to be the one who cleans up.
The day's holiness began with yesterday's ashes, cleared first, and cleared gladly.

how: The lifting of the ashes, terumat ha-deshen, is described in the Mishnah's tractates Tamid and Yoma, and some prayer books include its passages among the morning readings about the Temple service.

games.q: you're a priest in the Second Temple at dawn. the right to clear yesterday's ashes is up for grabs. what do the priests do?
o: avoid it: it's the dirtiest job.
race each other up the ramp to win it.

practice: Picture the space where you'll be today, your desk, your kitchen, your car, your inbox, and find one small patch of what's left from yesterday.
Picture clearing it carefully, as the first act of the day, not a chore to resent but the job that makes room for what's new. If there's inner ash too, an old irritation, notice it, and set it down.
